title: The Quarter of an Hour: Grüningen, the Sickroom at Jena, and the Making of the Beloved Dead
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Schloss Grüningen, the birth of Sophie von Kühn
stops.date_confidence: Date attested: de.wikipedia 'Sophie von Kühn' and the memorial medallion in the village church both give 17 March 1782. The birthplace is reconstruction; no consulted source names where she was born, and Grüningen is inferred from the family seat her father rebuilt in 1772.
stops.campa: Christiane Wilhelmine Sophie von Kühn is born on the seventeenth of March, 1782, in the corn country below Greußen, where her father Johann Georg von Kühn rebuilt the castle ten years earlier. The village is a scatter of roofs on the Helbe; the castle is its one large building. Fifteen years and two days are allotted to her. Almost everything the world will keep of her is written down by other people, most of it after she is dead, and most of it by men who never once saw her face.
suggested_refs: Schloss Grüningen, Ortsteil of Greußen, Kyffhäuserkreis, Thuringia
The Kirchenbuch of St. Petri, Grüningen, unconsulted, which would settle the birthplace

stops.name: Schloss Grüningen, the stepfather's household
stops.date_confidence: Rockenthien acquired Grüningen and Niedertopfstedt by marrying the widow in late 1786 (de.wikipedia, 'Rockenthien'). No exact date is given; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Her father is dead. Her mother, Sophie Wilhelmine, marries Captain Johann Rudolph von Rockenthien, who takes over Grüningen and Niedertopfstedt; the castle itself stands entailed to her two underage brothers as the fiefholders. The house fills with children: Friederike, Karoline, George and Hans von Kühn, the half-sister Wilhelmine from her father's first marriage, and the Rockenthien half-siblings after. The household is loud and unbookish, and it keeps an open table: men travelling on district business are put up for the night without ceremony.
suggested_refs: Johann Rudolph von Rockenthien, captain, stepfather and householder

stops.name: Niedertopfstedt, the entailed estate
stops.date_confidence: Named beside Grüningen as the property her dead father left, entailed to her two underage brothers (de.wikipedia, 'Rockenthien'). No source places Sophie herself there; the stop is reconstruction and the date follows the 1786 remarriage.
stops.campa: Three miles north the second estate lies in the same flat country, named in the property record beside Grüningen as part of what her dead father left behind. It passes with her mother to Captain von Rockenthien in the remarriage of 1786, and is held for her two underage brothers, who are its legal heirs. Whether Sophie is ever carried there or ever sleeps in the house, no document consulted here says. She is part of the estate on paper. The pin marks ground no source puts her on.
suggested_refs: Niedertopfstedt, Kyffhäuserkreis, second estate of the von Kühn entail

stops.name: Schloss Oberwiederstedt, the birth of Hardenberg
stops.date_confidence: attested (de.wikipedia, 'Novalis'; de.wikipedia, 'Oberwiederstedt'). Pin inherited from novalis.journey.json.
stops.campa: Ten years before Sophie, in the county of Mansfeld, a boy is born to a Herrnhut-pious family of the lower nobility and christened Georg Philipp Friedrich von Hardenberg. He is the one who will make her famous, and he does not know she exists for twenty-two years. The manor stands sixty miles north of Grüningen, two childhoods running toward one quarter of an hour in a strange house. His name is sometimes given as Georg Friedrich Philipp; the attested order is Georg Philipp Friedrich.
suggested_refs: Schloss Oberwiederstedt, Mansfelder Land, now the Novalis Museum

stops.name: Lucklum, the uncle's commandery
stops.date_confidence: de.wikipedia 'Novalis' places him at Lucklum under his uncle 'als Zwölfjähriger'; he turned twelve in May 1784, and the day is unattested. The research pool's 'c. 1782' is refuted by that wording. Pin inherited from novalis.journey.json.
stops.campa: As a twelve-year-old the boy is sent to his uncle Friedrich Wilhelm von Hardenberg, Landkomtur of the Teutonic Order, at the commandery of Lucklum near Braunschweig: a large worldly house of libraries and hunting after the narrow devotion at home. He reads there. Sophie is two years old at Grüningen while this happens, and the two facts belong to the same year without yet belonging to each other. The pin holds because the man who will invent her afterlife is being made in this house.
suggested_refs: Deutschordenskommende Lucklum, Ortsteil of Erkerode, Landkreis Wolfenbüttel

stops.name: Eisleben, the Gymnasium in Luther's town
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (de.wikipedia, 'Novalis'); month and day taken from novalis.journey.json, which pins 1790-06-01. No source consulted gives a day.
stops.campa: He enters the Prima of the Gymnasium at Eisleben under Rektor Christian David Jani. The town is Luther's, birth and death both, and the boy passing through its school comes off the same Saxon ground on the same pattern: a hushed religious household, and out of it a private revelation. Novalis only passes through its schoolroom on the way to the law faculty at Jena. Four years remain before Grüningen. Sophie is eight.
suggested_refs: The Gymnasium at Lutherstadt Eisleben under Christian David Jani

stops.name: Jena, the law faculty and Schiller's sickroom
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (de.wikipedia, 'Novalis'); the October pin is inherited from novalis.journey.json, which records the Jena year as 1790-91.
stops.campa: He begins law at Jena, the first of three universities. Schiller lectures here and falls ill, and the student helps nurse him; in this same town, in July 1794, Goethe and Schiller begin the friendship that organizes German letters for a decade. Jena comes back into Sophie's story as the city of her three operations, and later as the room where the men who make her a legend sit together. He is eighteen. She is eight years old and has never left Thuringia.
suggested_refs: The University of Jena, 1790-91
Schiller's illness of 1791 and the students who nursed him

stops.name: Leipzig, the friendship with Friedrich Schlegel
stops.date_confidence: Sources give 1791-1792 (de.wikipedia, 'Novalis'); the October pin is inherited from novalis.journey.json. No day attested.
stops.campa: Law again, and the friendship that will matter more than the law: Friedrich Schlegel, met here, who will edit the journal that first prints the poems her death produces, and who will stand at Hardenberg's own deathbed ten years later. Nothing in this year touches Sophie. It stands here because nearly every name that will be in the room when her legend is assembled is a name he collects before he has ever heard of her. Leipzig will print her death notice too.
suggested_refs: The University of Leipzig, 1791-92
Friedrich Schlegel, editor of the Athenäum

stops.name: Wittenberg, the law degree
stops.date_confidence: Sources give 1793-1794 (de.wikipedia, 'Novalis'); the June pin is inherited from novalis.journey.json. No day attested.
stops.campa: He finishes his legal studies at Wittenberg, Luther's other town, and takes the degree that qualifies him for the district office at Tennstedt. After that, nine miles of flat Thuringian road will separate his desk from her house. The education ends and the posting begins. The quarter of an hour is four months away. Sophie is twelve years old, and no source consulted here records a single thing about her education, her reading, or her health in this year or in any year before the next one.
suggested_refs: The University of Wittenberg, law faculty, 1793-94

stops.name: Bad Tennstedt, the clerk to Coelestin August Just
stops.date_confidence: de.wikipedia 'Novalis' and 'Bad Tennstedt' give October 1794 for his entry into service as Aktuarius; the day is unattested. Contradiction flagged: novalis.journey.json pins the same posting at 1794-11-01. Coordinate inherited from that file.
stops.campa: He enters service as Aktuarius under the Kreisamtmann Coelestin August Just, a decent man who becomes his friend and later his first biographer. The post is small, the district is small, and the district contains the Rockenthien house at Grüningen, where an official on business is fed and put up for the night. Nothing mystical arranges the meeting that is coming; a salt-and-taxes appointment in a flat country arranges it, in October, with a month to spare.
suggested_refs: Coelestin August Just, Kreisamtmann of Tennstedt and early biographer of Novalis

stops.name: Schloss Grüningen, the first meeting
stops.date_confidence: attested: de.wikipedia 'Sophie von Kühn' and 'Schloss Grüningen (Thüringen)' both give 17 November 1794 and both ages. Contradiction flagged: en.wikipedia 'Novalis' dates the meeting to 1795, which the October 1794 posting and the two German articles refute.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of November, 1794, a business trip brings the twenty-two-year-old clerk to Grüningen, where he is introduced to the twelve-year-old daughter of the house. He is in her company perhaps a quarter of an hour. A few days later he writes to his brother Erasmus that a quarter of an hour has decided him. That letter does not survive. The words survive only because Erasmus, who thought his brother had lost his reason, quoted them back at him in order to argue against them.
stops.quote: You write me that a quarter hour has determined you; how can you see through a girl in a quarter of an hour? All the more so a girl with such exceptional qualities as you describe to me? If you had written 'a quarter of a year' your talent for knowing the feminine heart would still have amazed me, but a quarter hour, just think of it yourself, a quarter hour sounds too miraculous.
stops.quote_source: Erasmus von Hardenberg, replying to his brother's now-lost letter; Novalis, Schriften IV, 367, translated in Wm. O'Brien, Novalis: Signs of Revolution (Duke University Press, 1995), 50
sources: Wm. O'Brien, Novalis: Signs of Revolution (Duke University Press, 1995), 49-50
suggested_refs: Novalis, Schriften IV, 367, the reply of Erasmus von Hardenberg

stops.name: Schloss Grüningen, the unofficial engagement
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction carried, not resolved: de.wikipedia ('Novalis', 'Sophie von Kühn') gives 15 March 1795, shortly before her thirteenth birthday; en.wikipedia ('Sophie von Kühn', 'Novalis') gives 17 March 1795, the birthday itself. The German date is pinned and the English one recorded.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of March, 1795, two days short of her thirteenth birthday, an unofficial engagement is made in the house. He is twenty-two, and nobody present records finding this remarkable. Between the engagement and the illness he rides over from Tennstedt whenever the office lets him go, a pattern well attested in the biography and itemized by no source consulted here. The spring and summer of 1795, he says long afterward, are the springtime of his life.
sources: Wm. O'Brien, Novalis: Signs of Revolution (Duke University Press, 1995), 36
suggested_refs: The unofficial engagement of March 1795, dated differently in German and English sources

stops.name: Schloss Grüningen, the diary: nothing happened
stops.date_confidence: O'Brien prints the entry under 1 March. Only the 11 March entry is tied to the year 1795 in any source reached; the year on this one is reconstruction from the engagement season, and the assignment is flagged rather than hidden.
stops.campa: She keeps a diary in these weeks. It is short, flat, and almost entirely about whether Hardenberg came. She spells his name as it sounds to her, differently on different days, and abbreviates it when she is bored. The Sophie of the Romantic literature is a transparent creature of light; the Sophie of her own handwriting is a girl noting that a visitor arrived and the day contained nothing. Both versions are on the record, and only one of them was written down by her.
stops.quote: Today Hartenberch visited again nothing happened.
stops.quote_source: Sophie von Kühn's diary, entry of 1 March, in Wm. O'Brien, Novalis: Signs of Revolution (Duke University Press, 1995), as reproduced on en.wikipedia, 'Sophie von Kühn'
sources: Wm. O'Brien, Novalis: Signs of Revolution (Duke University Press, 1995)
suggested_refs: Novalis, Schriften IV, 586f., the text of Sophie's diary, not consulted directly

stops.name: Schloss Grüningen, the diary: we were all alone
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and the year: O'Brien 1995, p. 54, entry of 11 March 1795, translating Novalis, Schriften IV, 586f. Wording verified twice by full-text search inside archive.org item novalissignsofre01obri.
stops.campa: The entries run on through the month in one key: the eleventh, then the twelfth like the eleventh, nothing at all happening on either day. The English Wikipedia article drops a word from the eleventh of March, printing that they were alone where O'Brien's translation reads that they were all alone. The second version means the household party; the first means the two of them by themselves. Longer romances have been hung on smaller hinges, and the wording used here is O'Brien's.
stops.quote: We were all alone today and nothing at all happened.
stops.quote_source: Sophie von Kühn's diary, entry of 11 March 1795, in Wm. O'Brien, Novalis: Signs of Revolution (Duke University Press, 1995), 54, translating Novalis, Schriften IV, 586f.
sources: Wm. O'Brien, Novalis: Signs of Revolution (Duke University Press, 1995), 54
suggested_refs: archive.org item novalissignsofre01obri, full text of O'Brien 1995

stops.name: Schloss Grüningen, the diary: repentance day
stops.date_confidence: O'Brien prints the entry under 13 March; the year 1795 is carried over from the 11 March entry and is reconstruction here. Open question, unresolved: 'repentance day' renders Buß- und Bettag, which in the Saxon and Prussian calendars of the period ordinarily fell in November. No source consulted addresses the discrepancy.
stops.campa: On the thirteenth she writes that it was repentance day and that Hardenberg was there; on the fourteenth, that he was still there and had a letter from his brother. The brother is Erasmus, who has been arguing by post against the whole business since the previous November. Two records of the same fortnight survive. His is ecstatic and will become a literature. Hers is four lines long, and says that a man came to the house and then that he was still in it.
stops.quote: Today was repentance day and Hartenb. was here.
stops.quote_source: Sophie von Kühn's diary, entry of 13 March, in Wm. O'Brien, Novalis: Signs of Revolution (Duke University Press, 1995), as reproduced on en.wikipedia, 'Sophie von Kühn'. 'Hartenb.' is her own abbreviation for Hardenberg.
sources: Wm. O'Brien, Novalis: Signs of Revolution (Duke University Press, 1995)
suggested_refs: The Saxon Buß- und Bettag calendar, against which the March dating of this entry has not been checked

stops.name: Schloss Grüningen, the consent of her parents
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia 'Novalis' gives the year 1795 and places the consent later than the March engagement; month and day are unknown and default to 01, which puts the pin earlier in the year than the event it records. Stated rather than smoothed.
stops.campa: Her mother and stepfather give their consent in the course of 1795. Rockenthien, a captain who married into the property and keeps an open table, sees no difficulty in it. The Hardenbergs see a great deal: a pious Herrnhut family of the old nobility, unwilling to bless their eldest son's attachment to a thirteen-year-old girl of no learning out of a loud house in the corn country. They withhold their blessing for two years. Their own approval arrives in the month she dies.
suggested_refs: The Rockenthien household's consent, 1795, undated within the year

stops.name: Weißenfels, the post at the salt works
stops.date_confidence: de.wikipedia 'Novalis': 'Januar 1796 wurde er Akzessist bei der Salinendirektion in Weißenfels'; day unattested. Contradiction carried: en.wikipedia dates the appointment as auditor to January 1797, a year later. The German date is followed because it explains why he was not at Grüningen when she died. Pin inherited from novalis.journey.json.
stops.campa: He moves to Weißenfels in January 1796 as Akzessist at the salt-works directorate, a salaried post in the state monopoly, taken to make the marriage possible. The consequence is geographic: he is fifty miles from Grüningen through the surgeries and the dying, and he is not in the room for any of it. He is twenty-three. The whole afterlife of Sophie von Kühn is built by a man who was somewhere else, at work, when the thing he built it out of was happening.
suggested_refs: The Salinendirektion at Weißenfels, employer of Novalis from January 1796

stops.name: Schloss Grüningen, the illness declares itself
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested (de.wikipedia and en.wikipedia, 'Sophie von Kühn'; anthrowiki.at); day unattested and defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: In November 1795 she falls ill at Grüningen: an inflammation of the liver, understood at the time as bound up with consumption of the lungs. She appears to recover. The remission does not hold. She is thirteen. From this month forward every document about her is a medical document or a document of grief, and the girl who wrote that nothing happened has no further entry in her own hand that any source consulted here reproduces. She is fourteen when the winter ends.
suggested_refs: The liver tumour and pulmonary tuberculosis diagnosed at Grüningen, November 1795

stops.name: Jena, three operations without anesthesia
stops.date_confidence: The span May to July 1796 is attested (de.wikipedia and en.wikipedia, 'Sophie von Kühn'); the three operations are not individually dated and the pin sits at the opening of the span. The clinic or house is named by no source consulted, so the coordinate marks the city. Contradiction carried on the surgeon: Johann Christian Stark the Elder in the research pool, Justus Christian Loder in novalis.journey.json. Neither is chosen.
stops.campa: Between May and July 1796 she is carried to Jena and cut three times, without anesthesia, for a tumour of the liver. She is fourteen. The operations are survived and are useless. Novalis comes to the town in agony and can do nothing there but wait. Two names for the surgeon stand in the record and neither is chosen over the other: Johann Christian Stark the Elder in one line of sources, Justus Christian Loder in another line kept for Novalis himself. Both were real Jena medical men.
suggested_refs: Johann Christian Stark the Elder, Jena
Justus Christian Loder, Jena
The surgical practice of 1796, before anesthesia

stops.name: Jena, the young idealists around Fichte
stops.date_confidence: Date and place inherited from fichte.journey.json, which names Novalis among the young idealists gathering at Jena in June 1796. Day is the file's convention, not an attested day.
stops.campa: In the same June, in the same town, the young idealists gather around Johann Gottlieb Fichte, and Fichte's own file names Novalis among them. Three months after the diagnosis and nine months before the death, the philosophy that will let him call her dying a doorway is being handed to him in the city where she is being opened up. The two facts sit at one coordinate in one month. Nothing in either record says that he ever set them side by side, though they are set side by side here anyway.
suggested_refs: Fichte's Jena lectures and the circle of 1796

stops.name: Schloss Grüningen, the Hardenbergs consent at last
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The only source is en.wikipedia 'Novalis', which says the approval came shortly before her death; the month is inferred from that phrase and the day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: His parents give their formal approval of the engagement shortly before she dies. One source carries this and no more, and the month is a reconstruction from the phrase shortly before. What the approval is worth by then is a question the record leaves standing: she has been cut three times and is not recovering, and the wedding it permits will not take place. The family that withheld its blessing for two years spends it on a girl with days to live.
suggested_refs: The Hardenberg family's approval of the engagement, March 1797, undated

stops.name: Schloss Grüningen, the death of Sophie von Kühn
stops.date_confidence: attested: de.wikipedia and en.wikipedia 'Sophie von Kühn'; de.wikipedia 'Novalis'; the date is repeated on the memorial medallion in the village church.
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of March, 1797, two days after her fifteenth birthday, Sophie von Kühn dies at Schloss Grüningen. Novalis is at Weißenfels. She has been engaged two years, ill sixteen months, and cut open three times; she leaves behind four lines about a visitor and nothing else in her own voice. The German Romantic cult of the beloved dead begins in this room, in a house belonging to a captain with an open table, in a village of one large building.
suggested_refs: The death chamber at Schloss Grüningen, 19 March 1797

stops.name: Leipzig, the notice in the Leipziger Zeitung
stops.date_confidence: attested: de.wikipedia 'Sophie von Kühn' gives the Leipziger Zeitung notice of 25 March 1797. Coordinate inherited from novalis.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of March the Rockenthien family's announcement of the death appears in the Leipziger Zeitung. It is the first time her name travels: a private girl in a village becoming a public fact in a few lines of newsprint paid for by her stepfather. Everything else printed about her for the next two centuries will be printed by other people for reasons of their own. Leipzig is also the town where the man who will print those reasons was first met.
suggested_refs: Leipziger Zeitung, 25 March 1797, death notice of the Rockenthien family

stops.name: Grüningen, St. Petri: the burial
stops.date_confidence: The burial in the Grüningen churchyard is attested by the medallion inscription in the wall of the village church of St. Petri (de.wikipedia, 'Schloss Grüningen (Thüringen)'; de.wikipedia, 'Sophie von Kühn'). No source consulted gives the date of burial, so the year of death stands with month and day defaulted. The same source states that the exact grave is unknown.
stops.campa: She is buried in the churchyard of the village church of St. Petri at Grüningen. The evidence is a medallion set later into the church wall, which gives her name, her two dates, and her one relation to history: the bride of the poet Friedrich von Hardenberg. The exact grave is not known, and the source that records the burial says so in the same breath. She lies somewhere in a small yard in Thuringia; the ground closed over the position without closing over the fact.
stops.quote: Auf diesem Gottesacker ruht Sophie von Kühn, geb. 17. März 1782, gest. 19. März 1797 auf Schloß Grüningen. Die Braut des Dichters Friedrich von Hardenberg (Novalis).
stops.quote_source: Memorial medallion set into the wall of the village church of St. Petri, Grüningen, quoted in de.wikipedia, 'Schloss Grüningen (Thüringen)'
suggested_refs: The Gedenktafel in the wall of the Dorfkirche St. Petri, Grüningen
The parish register of St. Petri, unconsulted, which would give the burial date

stops.name: Kirchberg, Grüningen: the vision of 13 May 1797
stops.date_confidence: attested: de.wikipedia 'Hymnen an die Nacht' quotes the journal entry of 13 May 1797 in full. What is contested is the inference, not the date: the same source reports that current scholarship argues against dating the composition of the Third Hymn to 1797, since no preliminary versions exist and the memory was reworked later into an initiation narrative.
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of May, 1797, he walks out in the evening to the grave-mound on the Kirchberg and writes down what happens there: indescribable joy, flashes of enthusiasm, centuries passing like moments, her nearness palpable, the grave blown away like dust in front of him. It is the founding document of the German night. Scholarship now doubts that the Third Hymn was composed out of it in 1797; no drafts survive, and the memory appears to have been worked up afterwards.
stops.quote: Abends ging ich zu Sophieen. Dort war ich unbeschreiblich freudig – aufblitzende Enthusiasmus Momente – Das Grab blies ich wie Staub, vor mir hin – Jahrhunderte waren wie Momente – ihre Nähe war fühlbar – ich glaubte sie solle immer vortreten.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Tagebuch, entry of 13 May 1797, quoted in de.wikipedia, 'Hymnen an die Nacht'
suggested_refs: Bruce Donehower, The Birth of Novalis: Friedrich von Hardenberg's Journal of 1797 (SUNY Press, 2007), not consulted here

stops.name: Weißenfels, the death of Erasmus von Hardenberg
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction carried, unresolved. en.wikipedia 'Novalis' gives the interval as four months after Sophie, i.e. July 1797; the verification pass for this file gives 14 April 1797, under four weeks, but could not produce a citable page in session and warns that de.wikipedia names only the father, Heinrich Ulrich Erasmus von Hardenberg (1738-1814), an easy confusion. The place of death is not attested; the pin at the family house is reconstruction.
stops.campa: Erasmus von Hardenberg, who argued against the engagement and was answered with a quarter of an hour, is dead of consumption in the same season. The interval is not settled: one line of sources puts his death four months after Sophie's, in July; a later verification pass puts it on the fourteenth of April, under four weeks after her, and could not produce a page to cite for it. Either way the journal of 1797 is written against a double bereavement, not a single one.
suggested_refs: Carl Wilhelm Erasmus von Hardenberg (b. 1774), brother and correspondent
A printed Novalis chronology, needed to settle the April or July question

stops.name: Freiberg, the Bergakademie
stops.date_confidence: de.wikipedia 'Novalis' gives 1797; en.wikipedia specifies the end of 1797, with matriculation in December. Contradiction recorded and treated as an error on one side: the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy places the mining studies just prior to Sophie's death, which both Wikipedias contradict. Pin inherited from novalis.journey.json.
stops.campa: At the end of 1797 he matriculates at the Bergakademie at Freiberg to study mining under Abraham Gottlob Werner, taking up his father's science and going down into the earth for a living. One encyclopedia places these studies just before Sophie's death; both Wikipedias place them after it, in December, and December is the reading followed here. The man who has just watched a grave blow away like dust becomes a mining engineer, and is good at it.
suggested_refs: Abraham Gottlob Werner and the Bergakademie Freiberg
W. A. Lampadius, chemistry at Freiberg

stops.name: Dresden, the Sistine Madonna
stops.date_confidence: Date and coordinate inherited byte-identical from novalis.journey.json, which pins the gallery visit with the Schlegels at July 1798. Day is that file's convention.
stops.campa: In July 1798 he stands in the picture gallery at Dresden with the Schlegels in front of Raphael's Sistine Madonna. What he sees there, by his own account, he sees through her: the sacred feminine of the painting read off a fifteen-year-old girl sixteen months dead in a Thuringian churchyard. This is the machinery of the myth working in public for the first time, in a gallery, in front of witnesses who agree with him and say so.
suggested_refs: Raphael, Sistine Madonna, Gemäldegalerie Dresden

stops.name: Freiberg, the second engagement
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: en.wikipedia 'Novalis' and 'Sophie von Kühn'; de.wikipedia 'Novalis'. Day unattested; pin inherited from novalis.journey.json.
stops.campa: In December 1798, at Freiberg, he becomes engaged a second time, to Julie von Charpentier, the daughter of one of his professors. It is a plain living attachment and it changes nothing in the writing. The dead girl keeps the poems; the living one gets the plans. Both files, his and hers, record the second engagement without recording any renunciation of the first, and he is still betrothed to Julie von Charpentier on the day he dies, two years and three months from this room.
suggested_refs: Julie von Charpentier, second fiancée, Freiberg

stops.name: Jena, Tieck and the writings of Jakob Böhme
stops.date_confidence: Date and coordinate inherited from jacob_boehme.journey.json and novalis.journey.json, which both place the Tieck meeting and the Böhme handoff at Jena in July 1799. Day is the files' convention.
stops.campa: In July 1799, at Jena, Ludwig Tieck puts the writings of Jakob Böhme into his hands, and the Böhme file records the handoff as the turn toward a mystical poetics. Tieck is also the man who will invent the public Sophie sixteen years later, in a preface. He never saw her. She had been dead more than two years when he met Hardenberg in this month, and everything he will ever write about her face he takes from a bereaved man's conversation in this town.
sources: Wm. O'Brien, Novalis: Signs of Revolution (Duke University Press, 1995), 35
suggested_refs: Ludwig Tieck's copy of Jakob Böhme, Jena 1799

stops.name: Jena, the Romantic gathering of November 1799
stops.date_confidence: attested and inherited from novalis.journey.json and schelling.journey.json. The Froebel and Hegel presences in the same town are attested in their own files; no meeting with Novalis is attested in any file, and those two lines are reconstruction.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of November, 1799, the Jena Romantics gather in one room: the Schlegel brothers, Caroline and Dorothea, Tieck, Schelling. Schelling has been professor here since October 1798 and will lose Auguste Böhmer to a fever in July 1800, a second young death mourned by the same friends. Froebel is a student in this town from October 1799 and Hegel arrives in 1801; no file attests that either met Novalis. Sophie is two and a half years dead and is the subject of the room.
suggested_refs: The Jena Romantikertreffen of 11 November 1799

stops.name: Weißenfels, assessor of the salt works
stops.date_confidence: de.wikipedia 'Novalis' confirms the December 1799 promotion to Assessor of the Salinen; day unattested. The additional word 'director', which comes from en.wikipedia's looser phrasing, is not supported by the German source and is dropped here.
stops.campa: In December 1799 he is made assessor of the salt works at Weißenfels. One English source calls him director as well; the German source supports assessor only, and the promotion is dropped accordingly. He is a competent salt official with a real career in a state monopoly, and the poems of the night are written in the hours left over from brine, seams, and accounts. The office matters because that is where the myth is actually made, in the evenings, by a working man.

stops.name: Berlin, the Athenäum prints the Hymns to the Night
stops.date_confidence: Year attested: first publication in the final issue of the Athenäum, Band 3, Stück 2, 1800, edited by August Wilhelm and Friedrich Schlegel at Berlin (de.wikipedia, 'Athenäum (Schlegel)' and 'Hymnen an die Nacht'). stops.campa: Hymnen an die Nacht is printed in 1800 in the last number of the Athenäum, the journal the Schlegel brothers run out of Berlin: six poems in prose and verse, the third of them lifting its phrases almost word for word out of the journal of 1797. No source consulted gives the month. It is not the only work he publishes in his lifetime, whatever the summaries say; Blüthenstaub and Glauben und Liebe are already in print, and it is the poetry that is new.

stops.name: Weißenfels, the blood in August
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested (en.wikipedia, 'Novalis'; novalis.journey.json); day defaulted. The cystic fibrosis suggestion is later scholarly conjecture and is carried as such.
stops.campa: In August 1800 he begins to cough blood. The diagnosis is consumption, the same word set beside Sophie's liver in 1795 and the same that took Erasmus; some later scholars suspect cystic fibrosis instead, on evidence the sources do not print. He is twenty-eight, with three years of work behind him and seven months of life ahead. The Night he has been addressing in print since the spring stops being a figure of speech and becomes a diagnosis in his own chest.

stops.name: Dresden, the hemorrhage and the failed cure
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested (en.wikipedia, 'Novalis'); day defaulted. Coordinate inherited from novalis.journey.json, which distinguishes this pin from the picture gallery.
stops.campa: After a severe hemorrhage in November he is taken to Dresden for treatment, the same city where he read the Sistine Madonna through her two years earlier. The cure does not hold and he comes back with nothing gained. This is the second time Dresden enters her story and the first time it enters without a painting in it. Julie von Charpentier is still his fiancée, and is not the person the poems written in these months understand him to be travelling toward.

stops.name: Weißenfels, appointed Supernumerar-Amtshauptmann
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: de.wikipedia 'Novalis' gives 6 December 1800 and the title Supernumerar-Amtshauptmann for the Thuringian district. The 'Amtmann' and the vague 'end of 1800' in the research pool are both corrected here.
stops.campa: On the sixth of December, 1800, he is appointed Supernumerar-Amtshauptmann for the Thuringian district: not Amtmann, and not vaguely at the end of the year, both of which an earlier draft had. He is a dying man being promoted. The state that employs him has no view about the poems and no reason to have one, and the appointment is the last ordinary thing that happens to him before the final three months begin. He signs for the district and coughs.

stops.name: Weißenfels, carried home to his parents' house
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested (en.wikipedia, 'Novalis'); day unattested and defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: In January 1801 he asks to be brought back to his parents' house at Weißenfels. He is carried home to the pious Herrnhut household that withheld its blessing from the engagement for two years and spent it in the month the girl died. He lies quiet. Those around him record no fear in him, which the later literature treats as the doctrine proving itself on the body of its author, and which was also, plainly, one of the ordinary ways that people die.

stops.name: Weißenfels, the death of Novalis
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia, 'Novalis'); pin inherited from novalis.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of March, 1801, four years and six days after Sophie, he dies at Weißenfels, twenty-eight years old, his brother playing the clavier in the next room and Friedrich Schlegel at the bedside. He leaves an unfinished novel, a body of fragments, and a fifteen-year-old girl fixed permanently in the position of the beloved dead. The Hymns had a little under a year in print while he was alive to watch anyone read them, and the rest of the work goes into other men's hands.

stops.name: Alter Friedhof, Weißenfels: the grave with an address
stops.date_confidence: Burial in the Alter Friedhof attested (en.wikipedia, 'Novalis'); the day 29 March is inherited from novalis.journey.json. No consulted source gives grave coordinates within the cemetery.
stops.campa: He is buried in the Alter Friedhof at Weißenfels on the twenty-ninth of March. Within a year Tieck and Friedrich Schlegel gather the papers and publish the Schriften, and out of that edition the whole nineteenth century takes its Novalis and, with him, its Sophie. Her grave at Grüningen is already unlocated. His has a cemetery, a stone, an address, and visitors; hers has a medallion in a wall saying that she is somewhere in that yard, without saying where.

stops.name: Berlin, Tieck's preface and the invention of Sophie
stops.date_confidence: The preface is Tieck's and dates from 1815 (S* I, xvi-xvii; reprinted Schriften IV, 552f.), translated in Wm. O'Brien, Novalis: Signs of Revolution (1995), 36. The place is reconstruction: the pin marks the Berlin publishing ground of the Schlegel circle, and no source consulted says where Tieck wrote it. The English wording circulating on Wikipedia as this passage is rejected here: untraceable to any printed edition and tagged 'citation needed' since April 2008.
stops.campa: In 1815 Ludwig Tieck writes the biographical preface to the Schriften and makes the Sophie the century will read: a face too finely made for this life, death or immortality staring out of the shining eyes. He is describing a type of child, in the plural, and applying it afterwards to a girl he never once saw. The passage is the origin of the myth and not evidence about her. He also puts her at thirteen completed years when Hardenberg met her, where the attested age is twelve.
stops.quote: and generally the sight of these transfigured and nearly transparent faces gives rise in us to the fear that they are too tender, too finely made for this life, that death or immortality stares out at us through their shining eyes; and our fearful foreboding is only too often confirmed by their speedy withering away.
stops.quote_source: Ludwig Tieck, biographical preface to Novalis, Schriften (1815), S* I, xvi-xvii, reprinted Schriften IV, 552f., translated in Wm. O'Brien, Novalis: Signs of Revolution (Duke University Press, 1995), 36

stops.name: Schloss Oberwiederstedt, the museum opens
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested (de.wikipedia, 'Oberwiederstedt'); day defaulted to 01. Coordinate inherited from novalis.journey.json.
stops.campa: In May 1989, after preservationists stop its planned demolition, the manor where he was born opens as the Novalis museum and a research centre for early Romanticism. The movement Sophie's death helped set in motion acquires an address, an archive, and a staff, in the last months of the state that had let the building go to ruin. Her name is spoken in every room of the place and not one of the rooms is hers or ever was; she came no closer to this house in her life than sixty miles, and she is the reason a good part of it is worth visiting.

stops.name: Weißenfels, Klosterstraße 24: the Novalis-Haus
stops.date_confidence: Present-day condition; the date is a placeholder for the current state, not an event. The address is attested: de.wikipedia 'Weißenfels' gives Klosterstraße 24, a building of 1680, city library below and Novalis museum above.
stops.campa: The Hardenberg family house at Klosterstraße 24 in Weißenfels, a building put up in 1680, holds the city library on the ground floor and the Novalis museum above it. The salt official's town keeps the poet. The rooms he was carried home to die in are open to visitors on ordinary weekday hours, and the girl whose death produced the work has no comparable room anywhere. She died at fifteen in a stepfather's house, and what she left behind is four lines of a diary.

stops.name: Grüningen, the house that carries her name
stops.date_confidence: Present-day condition; the date is a placeholder for the current state, not an event. The facts are attested: de.wikipedia 'Schloss Grüningen (Thüringen)' records the 1945 confiscation, the later nursing home, and the present name of the facility.
stops.campa: Schloss Grüningen, confiscated in 1945 and afterwards run as a nursing home, operates today as a care facility under the Novalis-Diakonie, and it is called Schloss Sophie von Kühn. The house where she was born, was engaged, fell ill and died spends its afterlife looking after the old and the sick under her name. The literal ending is the only one on record: the building took her name, kept the beds made, and went on working through two centuries and three states.
